subject: maths
title: Chapter 8 · Test 3
summary: Chapter 8 test 3: 15 questions on probability, Venn diagrams, two-way tables, conditional and independent events, tree diagrams and counting.
body: This test covers all of Chapter 8: probability review, Venn diagrams and two-way tables, conditional probability, independent events, tree diagrams with and without replacement, and counting techniques. It has 15 multiple-choice questions, from easy to challenge. Allow about 25 minutes, no notes, no calculator unless the question says. Draw a quick tree, table or set of boxes on scrap paper when it helps, and check that every probability you find is between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: A bag holds 6 blue, 2 red and 10 black pens. One is taken at random. What is the probability that it is NOT red?
questions.explanation: There are 18 pens and 16 are not red, so P = 16/18 = 8/9.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 1/9 is the probability that it IS red. Use the complement.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you counted colours (2 of 3 colours). Count the items, not the colours.
mistakes.D: Step 3: you divided by the 2 red pens. A probability is out of the total, 18.

questions.prompt: The Venn diagram shows 40 people and whether they chose Hockey and/or Soccer. One person is picked at random. Find P(Hockey ∪ Soccer).
questions.explanation: Hockey ∪ Soccer is everything inside the circles: 12 + 5 + 8 = 25, so P = 5/8.
steps: ∪ means "or": every region inside either circle.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 5 is the overlap, Hockey ∩ Soccer. ∪ means everything inside either circle.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you left out the overlap. People in both circles are in the union too.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 17 is the whole Hockey circle. Add the "Soccer only" region as well.

questions.diagram_alt: A Venn diagram with ξ = 40: Hockey only 12, both 5, Soccer only 8, and 15 outside both circles

questions.prompt: A fair coin is tossed and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of a head AND a number less than 3 on the die?
questions.explanation: The events are independent, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6. Adding the probabilities is the common slip.
steps: The two events don't affect each other: independent.

mistakes.B: Step 2: you added the probabilities. For "and" with independent events, multiply.
mistakes.C: Step 2: that is only the first event. Both must happen, so multiply by the second probability.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that is only the second event. Both must happen, so multiply by the first probability.

questions.prompt: A holiday package is made by choosing a place (5 options), a hotel (3 options) and a flight time (2 options), as shown by the boxes. How many different packages are possible?
questions.explanation: Multiplication principle: 5 × 3 × 2 = 30. Adding gives far too few.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added the choices. Each choice goes with every other choice — multiply.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you forgot the third choice (Flight). Multiply all three boxes.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you added the flight choices at the end. Every box multiplies.

questions.diagram_alt: Three boxes marked ? for the number of choices, labelled Place, Hotel and Flight, with multiplication signs between them

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the numbers added; the diagram shows every sum. What is the probability that the sum is 10 or more?
questions.explanation: 6 of the 36 equally likely cells fit (4+6, 5+5, 6+4, 5+6, 6+5, 6+6), so P = 6/36 = 1/6. The 11 sums are not equally likely.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you counted each pair once (e.g. only one of 1 + 5 and 5 + 1). Every cell is a different outcome — count all 6.
mistakes.B: Step 1: you used 3 of the 11 possible sums, but the sums are not equally likely. Use the 36 cells.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you put 6 cells over 11 sums. The total is the 36 equally likely cells.

questions.diagram_alt: A 6 by 6 grid with dice values 1 to 6 along the top and side; each cell shows the sum of the two values

questions.prompt: The two-way table has some blank cells. Complete it, then find the probability that a randomly chosen person from all 70 is in the "Weekend" row and the "On time" column (marked ?).
questions.explanation: Weekend / Late = 10 − 6 = 4, so the ? cell = 20 − 4 = 16 and P = 16/70 = 8/35.
steps: Divide by the grand total: P = 16/70 = 8/35.

mistakes.A: Step 3: you divided by the Weekend row total. The person is chosen from all 70.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 4 is the Weekend / Late cell. Go on to the On time column.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 60 is the whole On time column. You need the Weekend row only.

questions.diagram_alt: A two-way table with columns Late, On time, Total and rows Weekday, Weekend, Total. Weekday: Late 6, Total 50. Weekend: On time marked ?, Total 20. Total row: Late 10, grand total 70. Other cells blank

questions.prompt: Use the two-way table. A person in the "Outdoor" row is chosen at random. What is the probability that they are in the "Win" column?
questions.explanation: Given Outdoor, use only that row: 9 of its 20 are Win, so P = 9/20. Dividing by the grand total ignores the condition.
steps: Given "Outdoor": use only that row, 20 people.

mistakes.B: Step 1: you divided by all 40. Given "Outdoor", divide by that row's total.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you divided by the Win column — that is P(Outdoor | Win). The given group is the Outdoor row.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 23/40 ignores the condition. Use only the Outdoor row.

questions.diagram_alt: A two-way table with columns Win, Loss, Total and rows Indoor (14, 6, 20), Outdoor (9, 11, 20) and Total (23, 17, 40)

questions.topic: Tree diagrams with and without replacement
questions.prompt: A box has 5 milk and 3 dark chocolates. Two are taken without replacement. Find the probability that both are dark.
questions.explanation: Without replacement: 3/8 × 2/7 = 3/28. Using 3/8 twice forgets that the first one is not put back.
steps: Second pick: 7 left, 2 of the right type: 2/7.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 3/8 again is WITH replacement. One has gone, so use 2/7.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you changed the top but not the bottom. Only 7 are left.
mistakes.D: Step 3: you added the branches. Along a path, multiply.

questions.prompt: Seven runners line up in seven lanes, and the captain must be in lane 1. How many different line-ups are possible?
questions.explanation: Fix the restricted item (1 way), then arrange the other 6: 6! = 720. 7! ignores the rule.
steps: Fill the restricted position first: 1 way.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 7! counts every order. The fixed item has only 1 place.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you subtracted from the total, which counts the orders that break the rule.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 6 items are left, but they can be arranged in many orders — use a factorial.

questions.prompt: Of 36 people, 20 like tennis, 18 like golf and 4 like neither. A person is chosen at random. What is the probability that they like both?
questions.explanation: 36 − 4 = 32 are in at least one group, but 20 + 18 = 38, so 38 − 32 = 6 are counted twice: they are in both. P = 1/6.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 4 is the number in neither group. Use it to find the overlap.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 32/36 is P(at least one). "Both" is only the overlap.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 20 + 18 counts the "both" people twice — compare it with 32.

steps: Addition rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.28.

mistakes.B: Step 3: dividing by P(A) gives P(B | A). The given event is B.
mistakes.C: Step 2: that is P(A ∩ B). Divide it by P(B).
mistakes.D: Step 3: you divided by P(A ∪ B). Divide by the given event, P(B).

questions.topic: Tree diagrams with and without replacement
questions.prompt: A team plays two matches. P(wins match 1) = 0.5. If it wins match 1, P(wins match 2) = 0.75; if it loses match 1, P(wins match 2) = 0.3 (see the tree diagram). Find the probability that it wins exactly one match.
steps: Exactly one happens on two paths: Win then Lose, or Lose then Win.

mistakes.A: Step 3: that is only one path. The other order also gives exactly one — add both paths.
mistakes.C: Step 1: that path has two successes. You need exactly one.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 1 − P(none) is "at least one", which includes two successes.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram: first Win 0.5 and Lose 0.5; after Win, Win 0.75 and Lose 0.25; after Lose, Win 0.3 and Lose 0.7

questions.prompt: Three seeds are planted. Each sprouts with probability 0.2, independently. Find the probability that at least one sprouts.

mistakes.A: Step 2: that is the chance they ALL succeed. "At least one" is 1 − P(none).
mistakes.B: Step 3: that is P(none). Subtract it from 1.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you added the probabilities. Use 1 − P(none) for "at least one".

questions.prompt: 20% of emails are spam. The word "free" appears in 60% of spam emails and in 5% of other emails (see the tree diagram). An email contains "free". What is the probability that it is spam?

mistakes.A: Step 3: 0.6 is P(Free | Spam), the condition the wrong way round. Here Free is given.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 0.12 is P(Spam and Free). Divide it by P(Free).
mistakes.C: Step 3: that is P(Not spam | Free), the other branch. Use the Spam path on top.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram: first Spam 0.2 and Not spam 0.8; after Spam, Free 0.6 and No free 0.4; after Not spam, Free 0.05 and No free 0.95

questions.prompt: Two people are chosen at random from 10 volunteers to run a stall. What is the probability that Mei and Raj are the two chosen?
questions.explanation: Number of possible pairs = 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45, and only one of them is the pair wanted, so P = 1/45.
steps: Each pair is counted twice (in two orders), so there are 90 ÷ 2 = 45 pairs.
Only one pair is the one wanted: P = 1/45.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 10 × 9 counts ordered picks, but the pair can be picked in 2 orders. Divide by 2 first.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 2/10 is the chance that ONE particular person is chosen. Both must be chosen.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 10 × 10 lets the same person be picked twice. Count pairs of different people.
